item.title: Robotics Summit 2027 opens call for speakers
item.dc:creator: Steve Crowe
item.description:
The Robotics Summit & Expo returns to Boston June 2-3, 2027 with deepened coverage, an expanded expo floor, and more.

The post Robotics Summit 2027 opens call for speakers appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
The Robot Report invites you to submit a session abstract to be considered for presentation at the 2027 Robotics Summit & Expo, which will be on June 2-3 at the Hynes Convention Center in Boston. The Robotics Summit is the leading event focused on the technical issues involved with developing commercial robots.

The Robotics Summit & Expo will gather more than 5,000 attendees to explore the latest enabling technologies, engineering best practices, and emerging trends shaping commercial robotics. The event will feature five keynotes and over 60 educational sessions.

Attendees can connect with 250+ exhibitors and take advantage of networking opportunities, a Career Fair, a robotics development challenge, and the The Robot Report 50 Awards Gala.

Sessions should be technical and educational to help robotics engineers overcome common development challenges. Topics can be submitted based on the following tracks:

    • Technologies: Advances in core technologies common to all classes of commercial robots
    • Design, Development & Manufacturability: Technologies and methodologies to simulate, design, prototype and manufacture commercial robots for scale
    • AI: How machine learning, agentic robotics, foundation models and other AI technologies impact commercial robotics development
    • Coding & Programming: Learn about coding languages and new programming methodologies to help robotics engineers build smarter robots.
    • Logistics: Advances in warehouse robotics, key enabling technologies, and emerging applications
    • Healthcare Robotics: Advances in medical robotics, from surgical systems to patient care solutions, key enabling technologies, and emerging applications

Deadline for 2027 Robotics Summit & Expo

The deadline for submitting speaker proposals is December 30, 2026. To apply to deliver a session at the Robotics Summit & Expo click here.

All speakers will receive complimentary full conference registration with admission to all keynotes, sessions, panels, networking receptions, and special events. 

For information about sponsorship and exhibition opportunities, download the prospectus. Questions regarding sponsorship opportunities should be directed to Colleen Sepich at csepich[AT]arrowfly.com.

For questions regarding Robotics Summit conference programming, contact Steve Crowe at scrowe[AT]arrowfly.com.

The post Robotics Summit 2027 opens call for speakers appeared first on The Robot Report.

item.title: SoftBank acquires Marc Raibert’s Robotics and AI Institute
item.dc:creator: Steve Crowe
item.description:
SoftBank has completed its acquisition of the Robotics and AI Institute from Hyundai Motor Group, expanding its robotics portfolio as the research organization looks to fill 24 open positions in Massachusetts and Switzerland.

The post SoftBank acquires Marc Raibert’s Robotics and AI Institute appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
SoftBank has completed its acquisition of the Robotics and AI Institute (RAI) from Hyundai Motor Group, The Robot Report has learned. Financial terms of the deal were not disclosed. SoftBank responded to emailed questions from The Robot Report about the acquisition, but it declined to comment.

The Robot Report first reported the acquisition agreement in September 2026. The deal adds another prominent name to SoftBank’s growing portfolio of robotics companies.

Boston Dynamics founder Marc Raibert founded the RAI Institute in 2022 with more than $400 million in initial funding from Hyundai. Based in Cambridge, Mass., the institute focuses on solving fundamental challenges in robotics, including mobility, manipulation, perception, and intelligence.

RAI is also looking to expand its team. It currently has 24 open positions, including internships, across its offices in Cambridge and Zurich, Switzerland. The openings cover a range of technologies, including robot learning, manipulation, simulation, navigation, and hardware engineering.

SoftBank continues to build its robotics portfolio

The acquisition reunites SoftBank and Raibert. SoftBank acquired Boston Dynamics from Alphabet in 2017 before selling a controlling stake to Hyundai in 2021 in a deal that valued the robotics company at $1.1 billion.

Hyundai recently acquired SoftBank’s remaining 9.65% stake in Boston Dynamics, giving Hyundai Motor Group and its executive chairman full ownership of the robotics company. The deal marks the end of SoftBank’s nearly decade-long investment in Boston Dynamics.

SoftBank has since acquired or invested in a number of robotics companies, including 1X Technologies, Agile Robots, AutoStore, BALYO, Berkshire Grey, Brain Corp, Skild AI, and Symbotic.

It will be interesting to see how much collaboration takes place between the RAI and some of these companies. There are potential synergies, for example, between the research being done at the institute and the technologies being developed by Skild AI and Agile Robots.

It’s unclear whether SoftBank’s ownership will change the institute’s research priorities or whether it will continue to operate independently.

The deal also comes at a time when SoftBank’s planned $5.375 billion acquisition of ABB Robotics faces an uncertain future. Chinese regulators blocked the acquisition of ABB’s robotics business in China, putting the deal in jeopardy.

Simulated robots training on a tire-rolling skill in parallel. Each skill takes a few hours on a single GPU. | Credit: Robotics and AI Institute

The post SoftBank acquires Marc Raibert’s Robotics and AI Institute appeared first on The Robot Report.

item.title: How does Orchard AI fit into John Deere’s technology portfolio?
item.dc:creator: Brianna Wessling
item.description:
John Deere said the deal strengthens its ability to help growers make more informed decisions throughout the growing season.

The post How does Orchard AI fit into John Deere’s technology portfolio? appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
John Deere said Orchard AI’s plant-level crop insights will bring more precision to its technology. | Source: John Deere

John Deere has acquired Orchard AI, a San Francisco-based company that develops crop intelligence systems for high-value crop growers. Orchard AI uses vehicle-mounted, AI-powered cameras to capture data for every individual tree, vine, or plant across a farm.

The system analyzes hundreds of images per tree, giving growers a detailed view of crop conditions. It also gives accurate yield estimates, precise fruit counts, fruit size and color data, canopy measurements, and more. 

The company also offers its FruitScope software platform, which enables growers to visualize and use this data to make more informed farm management decisions.

“We started Orchard AI to give our growers the crop intelligence they need to help them farm more profitably and sustainably than ever before,” said Charlie Wu, the CEO of Orchard AI. “Everything that we do is in service of our growers, and joining John Deere lets us accelerate our mission. Together, we aim to bring the benefits of AI-powered crop intelligence to every grower across the globe.”

Submit your innovation now!

John Deere said the deal strengthens its ability to help growers make more informed decisions throughout the growing season. The company plans to combine Orchard AI’s plant-level crop insights with its own expertise in precision agriculture, equipment, and farm technology. 

“Everything we do starts with helping our customers succeed,” said Tim Marquis, the director of Farm Systems Innovation at John Deere. “This acquisition connects crop-level intelligence with John Deere technology and equipment that can precisely execute the work in the field. By bringing these capabilities together, we have an opportunity to help growers make more informed decisions across their operations and get more value from the technology they already rely on.”

Inside John Deere’s growing technology portfolio

By combining Orchard AI’s crop intelligence with Deere’s equipment and technology., the company said growers can better understand what their trees need and act at the right time. This acquisition is part of John Deere’s increasing focus on integrating advanced technologies into its portfolio. 

John Deere’s recent journey in acquiring robotics and AI companies started in 2017 when it acquired Blue River Technology for $305 million. Blue River Technology developed computer vision and machine learning technology that enables agricultural sprayers to identify weeds and selectively apply herbicides.

A few years later, it acquired Bear Flag Robotics for $250 million. Bear Flag retrofitted autonomy stacks onto existing tractors. The company used cameras, lidar, and radar technology to give tractors redundant, 360-degree situational awareness on farms. 

In January 2022, John Deere unveiled its first fully autonomous tractor, which incorporated some of the technologies it acquired over the years. The machine combined Deere’s 8R tractor, TruSet-enabled chisel plow, and GPS guidance system with new advanced technologies, Deere said at the time. 

After releasing its autonomous tractor, John Deere continued making acquisitions to fill out its technology stack. It acquired intellectual property from Light, which specializes in depth sensing and camera-based perception for autonomous vehicles, in May 2022.

In 2023, John Deere acquired SparkAI, a New York-based startup that developed human-in-the-loop technology to help robots resolve edge cases in real-time. 

Most recently, the company acquired GUSS Automation, a developer of autonomous sprayers, in 2025. The companies had already been working together for years, with John Deere being an exclusive provider of GUSS sprayers. The acquisition indicated John Deere’s interest in high-value crops, such as orchards and vineyards, which GUSS specializes in.

The post How does Orchard AI fit into John Deere’s technology portfolio? appeared first on The Robot Report.

item.title: Special Report: Engineering Focus on Motion Control
item.dc:creator: The Robot Report Staff
item.description:
The Robot Report looks at recent advances in automation for manufacturing, from improvements in technologies and use cases to the potential of humanoids and AI.

The post Special Report: Engineering Focus on Motion Control appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Motion control is at the heart of every robotic system. From industrial robotic arms and autonomous mobile robots (AMRs) to humanoids, the ability to move with precision, efficiency, and reliability is critical to successful development and deployment.
 
Developers must balance increasingly complex requirements around torque, speed, accuracy, weight, power consumption, and cost. Advances in motors, actuators, gearboxes, sensors, and software are helping engineers address these challenges and unlock new capabilities.
 
In its latest Engineering Focus on Motion Control report, The Robot Report examines the technologies, engineering challenges, and industry developments shaping the next generation of robotic systems.
 
This free, 32-page report features technical insights, industry analysis, and practical engineering guidance on topics including:
  • Designing motion control systems for humanoid robots
  • Advances in open-source motion planning software
  • Using motion-capture data to train robots
  • Selecting the right motion control architecture
  • Manufacturing gearboxes for humanoids at scale
  • Choosing brushless DC motors for robotic arms and mobile robots
The report also features insights from leading motion control technology providers on force sensing, dexterous manipulation, compact actuators, custom gearboxes, and the advantages and disadvantages of building versus buying motion control systems.
 
Whether you’re designing a new robotic platform, optimizing an existing system, or evaluating components for your next project, this report can help you make more informed engineering decisions and navigate the rapidly evolving motion control market.
 
Fill out the form to download your free copy of Engineering Focus on Motion Control from The Robot Report today.

 

 

The post Special Report: Engineering Focus on Motion Control appeared first on The Robot Report.

item.title: NVIDIA reinstates Jensen Huang after 11-day absence
item.dc:creator: Steve Crowe
item.description:
The NVIDIA board reversed its decision following discussions with Huang and senior U.S. government officials, amid growing pressure from the White House, investors and technology executives.

The post NVIDIA reinstates Jensen Huang after 11-day absence appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
So much for robotics being in its post-Jensen Huang era. Just 11 days after his resignation amid allegations of personal misconduct and concerns about potential national security risks involving China, NVIDIA has reinstated Jensen Huang as president and CEO.

The company announced today that its board of directors unanimously voted to bring Huang back. Huang also returns to NVIDIA’s board, effective immediately.

NVIDIA said the board was satisfied with Huang’s candor and ability to lead the company. It also consulted with senior U.S. government officials before determining that his reinstatement poses no national security risk.

“The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” said Harvey Jones, NVIDIA’s board chair.

The decision marks a dramatic reversal for NVIDIA. During the company’s earnings call on Nov. 17, Jones explicitly ruled out bringing Huang back, saying the board had unanimously accepted his resignation and did not intend to reinstate him. Just six days later, the board unanimously voted to restore Huang to the position he had held since co-founding NVIDIA in 1993.

The reversal followed growing pressure from President Donald Trump, NVIDIA employees, investors and prominent technology executives. Trump publicly supported Huang’s potential return on Nov. 16, saying he would not object to his reinstatement. On Sunday, Nov. 22, Trump again urged NVIDIA’s board to bring Huang back.

Submit your innovation now!

Meanwhile, a “Stand With Jensen” petition attracted more than 200,000 signatures, including support from current and former NVIDIA employees, investors and technology leaders such as Elon Musk and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney.

NVIDIA also faced considerable financial uncertainty following Huang’s departure, with its market value falling sharply and questions emerging about who could replace an executive who had led the company for more than three decades.

It remains unclear precisely what persuaded the board to reverse course. NVIDIA did not identify which government officials were consulted or disclose what information they provided. The company also did not say whether the public campaign influenced its decision.

Colette Kress, who served as interim CEO following Huang’s resignation, will continue in her role as chief financial officer. Jones will remain board chair.

“I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” Huang said. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment.”

Huang also thanked NVIDIA’s board, employees, shareholders and his family for their support, adding, “I can’t wait to get back to work.”

National security investigation continues

Huang’s reinstatement does not end the scrutiny surrounding his departure. NVIDIA said an independent board committee will continue investigating reports that Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort.

The committee has retained independent counsel, and Huang has committed to cooperating fully with the investigation. NVIDIA also recently established a National Security and Export Control Committee composed entirely of independent directors. The committee will oversee trade compliance and national security risks, with support from legal counsel and national security specialists.

The company did not provide a timeline for completing its internal investigation.

Huang’s return brings back robotics’ biggest champion

Huang’s return also restores one of the robotics industry’s most visible advocates to the helm of a company that has become increasingly important to robot development.

As The Robot Report previously examined, Huang has spent years promoting robotics and physical AI as major long-term opportunities. He has regularly featured robots in NVIDIA’s keynote presentations and helped bring greater attention to the industry’s potential.

Under his leadership, NVIDIA expanded its robotics portfolio with technologies including Isaac Sim, Isaac Lab, GR00T foundation models, Isaac ROS and Jetson computing platforms.

NVIDIA has also invested in and partnered with robotics developers, including humanoid companies, as it works to establish its technology as a foundation for robot training, simulation and deployment.

The post NVIDIA reinstates Jensen Huang after 11-day absence appeared first on The Robot Report.

item.title: The manufacturing data gap holding back physical AI
item.dc:creator: Mike Kenworthy, CTO, VulcanForms
item.description:
Manufacturers looking to deploy autonomous robots must close gaps in industrial data collection, interoperability, and quality feedback to enable reliable decision-making and improve production efficiency.

The post The manufacturing data gap holding back physical AI appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Robotics and physical AI companies have raised nearly $48 billion so far in 2026, but the rollout of fully autonomous machines in industrial settings isn’t a given. For robots to step beyond controlled environments onto the manufacturing floor, they need real-world data to learn from.

Most production facilities aren’t set up to provide it.

Consider the welding process. For a robot to improve its technique autonomously, it needs to understand how changes in welding angle, travel speed, workpiece position, and other key parameters affect the finished result. Experienced technicians develop this understanding through years of hands-on experience, but much of that knowledge isn’t captured in a form robotics partners can use to train autonomous systems.

Similar gaps exist in other manufacturing processes where technicians rely on experience to make adjustments that aren’t consistently documented.
Manufacturers looking to deploy physical AI need to close this data gap. Without information connecting process decisions to production outcomes, even sophisticated robotic systems may struggle to adapt to changing conditions.

These limitations could prevent manufacturers from achieving the efficiency and quality improvements they expect from physical AI.

Why industrial data remains a barrier to physical AI

Manufacturers already collect extensive operational data, but much of it was never structured for autonomous learning. Sometimes it is collected and never even reviewed at all!

Relevant contextual information often sits in separate systems. A machine may record operating parameters while a quality management system captures inspection results, making it difficult to connect process decisions with finished-part quality.

Manufacturing leaders are increasingly aware that these silos are an obstacle. According to the Manufacturing Leadership Council’s 2026 Smart Factories and Digital Production Survey, 37% of surveyed manufacturers cited a lack of data interoperability as a major roadblock to implementing their smart factory strategies, up from 22% in 2025.

However, improving interoperability alone won’t get robots the data they need to learn. Manufacturers also need to ensure that production records can be tied to measurable quality outcomes.

Submit your innovation now!

3 ways manufacturers can prepare for physical AI

Preparing a factory for physical AI requires more than collecting additional data or connecting disparate systems. Manufacturers need to understand what information their robotic systems will rely on, how that data reflects real production conditions and whether it can help systems make reliable adjustments over time.

Addressing these questions early, in collaboration with robotics partners, can help manufacturers identify gaps in their existing infrastructure and focus investments where they’ll have the greatest impact.

Here are three areas to prioritize before deployment.

1. Capture data that reflects real production conditions

Begin by identifying the production conditions your robotic systems need to recognize and respond to. Focus on capturing the complex interactions between the process parameters and quality outcomes to show how planned and unplanned changes in materials or equipment performance affect the finished product.

Consider metal additive manufacturing, where factors like powder (or wire) characteristics, processing temperatures, and environmental conditions can influence a component’s final properties and characteristic defect structure. Connecting these variables with inspection results gives your robotics partners a clearer picture of which conditions contribute to defects or variations in quality.

You can then use that information to train systems to recognize changing production conditions and develop more realistic simulations for testing their responses.

2. Connect data across the entire production process

The data you capture won’t have much value if it remains isolated within individual machines or production stages. The next step is to create a digital thread that connects production conditions with inspection results and finished-part quality.

I’ve seen this challenge firsthand in advanced manufacturing. AI-based image recognition is becoming table stakes for assessing quality within metal additive manufacturing printers, while downstream equipment such as heat-treatment furnaces may be far more difficult to integrate into the same system. Lior Susan of Eclipse rightly says: “If your physical asset isn’t generating real-time operational data, it’s a dead asset.”

The disconnect creates gaps in the production history of a component, making it harder to understand how subsequent processing affects its final properties.

To close those gaps, you need to connect equipment and quality management systems that weren’t designed to communicate. Start by identifying the data needed for a specific robotic application, then work with technology partners to establish consistent part identifiers and link process records to inspection results in a true digital thread.

By starting with a targeted application, you can build the data connections to support physical AI without having to overhaul your entire production infrastructure at once.

Submit your innovation now!

3. Build feedback loops around quality and repeatability

Finally, establish how autonomous systems will be evaluated and when human oversight is required. Work with your robotics partners to identify which process adjustments can be made automatically and how the system will determine whether those changes improved production outcomes.

In medical device manufacturing, for example, regulatory requirements often mandate validation of production processes to ensure consistent product quality. Changes to those processes may require additional testing and revalidation, limiting how freely AI systems can modify production parameters.

Before authorizing autonomous adjustments, work with your robotics partners to define acceptable operating limits and establish how the system will verify results.

Also develop clear criteria for when an unexpected outcome requires engineering review. A system that can modify operating parameters but can’t evaluate the resulting quality is not ready to make those decisions independently.

Preparing manufacturing data for industrial autonomy

As you evaluate data infrastructure investments, determine whether they will support your physical AI goals. Before adding more sensors or connecting another piece of equipment, have a plan for how the resulting information will help explain how a process adjustment affects product quality.

Where that connection is missing, you may get more value from linking existing process records to inspection results than from collecting additional machine data.

Industrial autonomy won’t depend on how much data manufacturers collect, but on whether their robotic systems are actually leveraging that data to make reliable decisions on the factory floor.

About the author

Michael Kenworthy is chief technology officer at VulcanForms, bringing more than a decade of experience in engineering, product development and advanced manufacturing. Previously, he served as VP of engineering at Relativity Space, where he helped lead the development of 3D-printed rockets, and chief product officer at Seurat Technologies, where he oversaw product strategy. He holds degrees from MIT and the University of Wisconsin-Madison.

The post The manufacturing data gap holding back physical AI appeared first on The Robot Report.

item.title: Medtronic’s Hugo surgical robot ready for bigger operation
item.dc:creator: Brianna Wessling
item.description:
Globally, the Hugo surgical system is on track to surpass 50,000 cumulative procedures by the end of Medtronic's fiscal year. 

The post Medtronic’s Hugo surgical robot ready for bigger operation appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Medtronic’s Hugo surgical robot features a modular design that allows surgeons to use only the robotic arms needed for any given procedure. | Source: Medtronic

Medtronic this week announced the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has cleared the Hugo robotic-assisted surgery system for use in general surgery procedures. The approval enables the modular, cart-based system to perform surgeries across the abdomen.

The clearance covers all upper abdominal general surgical procedures, including cholecystectomy, Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, ventral hernia, and small bowel resection. The FDA also cleared lower abdominal procedures of inguinal hernia and appendectomy.

Combined, Medtronic said these procedures account for about 3.5 million surgeries annually in the U.S.

“We started our U.S. journey in February of last year,” Rajit Kamal, the general manager of robotic surgical technologies at Medtronic, told The Robot Report. “We have been pleased with the progress we have made. We are in many leading hospitals in the country with our urology indication. Our general surgery further opens those opportunities for us and for our combined value proposition, not just for Hugo, but in service, training, support, touch surgery, and the broader portfolio.”

Medtronic already has experience in many of these general surgery areas. The company said its technologies in open and laparoscopic approaches have been used for more than fifty years.

Medtronic leverages experience abroad in the approval process

Medtronic received CE marking for general surgery in Europe in 2022. This provided Medtronic with clinical data to support its U.S. submission. Globally, Hugo is on track to surpass 50,000 cumulative procedures by the end of the Medtronic fiscal year. 

“General surgery has been available on Hugo outside of the U.S., and it is our fastest-growing procedural mix, because we, as Medtronic, have a strong value proposition in general surgery,” Kamal said. “Many of [the surgeries] are multi-quadrant procedures where Hugo’s modularity provides better coverage, flexibility in port placement, and ability to reach the surgical sites.”

Medtronic gained FDA approval for urology, a more common segment for surgical robots, in December 2025. The company also conducted a U.S. clinical study of Hugo for hernia repair, announcing in September 2025 that the system had met the study’s safety and effectiveness endpoints.

At the same time, the company gained an investigational device exemption (IDE) to operate a clinical trial in the U.S. for general surgery.

“We took two pathways [to gain FDA clearance]. One was we did a clinical trial in the U.S. and worked with the FDA and IDE, but we also leveraged the data from outside the U.S,” Kamal said. “I think it was a creative way of approaching this, and we were able to get a broader set of general surgery indications.” 

General surgery also represents the highest growth for Hugo system procedures outside the U.S., surpassing urology and gynecology.

How is Medtronic using the latest advances in AI?

Outside of bringing its existing technology to new markets, Medtronic is also interesting in exploring new technologies. This includes the latest advances in AI, which dominate conversations in the robotics industry today.

Kamal said surgical care has three stages: preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative. He thinks AI can make a difference in each stage.

“Pre-operative, you could use AI to plan a procedure, using imaging and all that to personalize it. You use AI intraoperatively to be able to identify anatomic structures, to be able to identify critical structures, and to be able to provide intraoperative guidance. You can use AI post-operatively as well to optimize the post-op recovery pathway,” Kamal said.

In June, Medtronic gained FDA approval for its compute platform for the operating room, Touch Surgery Aide. The system brings AI insights to surgeons during surgical procedures. The platform uses computer vision and AI to analyze surgical video and provide real-time information to surgical teams.

“We clearly see AI playing a very important role. Our intent is to bring AI features onto our Hugo platform and continue being that partner with the surgeons to use AI to provide them insights and continue to make improvements in terms of the patient outcome,” Kamal said.

Robotics is changing how surgeons operate

One of the biggest impacts of robotic surgery is on the surgeons themselves. Conventional laparoscopic surgery can be physically demanding, requiring surgeons to stand for long periods while manipulating instruments. Robotic-assisted systems like Hugo allow surgeons to operate from a seated console, potentially reducing some of that physical strain.

“After decades of practicing, it takes a toll on their body. If you think about a robotic procedure, number one, you get a magnified 3D image, so you have clear depth perception. You’re sitting comfortably in a chair,” Kamal said.

Additionally, the controls are more intuitive than the traditional imaging systems a surgeon would use in a manual procedure. “Any laparoscopic surgeon who is doing robotics will tell you that they don’t want to go back,” Kamal continued. 

Robotics could also help newer surgeons develop their skills.

“If you’re a new surgeon coming in, just think about the amount of information you get if you are doing it robotically. You can see the surgical field much clearer,” Kamal said. “The instruments are a lot more precise and accurate. Now with AI, you get better features.”

What comes next for Medtronic?

Medtronic is continuing to make progress in the U.S. market. The company is running an IDE study for using Hugo in gynecology. The study evaluates Hugo’s safety and effectiveness when used during radical, modified radical or total hysterectomies, inclusive of those treated for malignancies.

The company is also investing in technologies that it hasn’t developed. In September, it invested $700 million into Cornerstone Robotics. With the deal, Medtronic also gained the rights to distribute Cornerstone Robotics’ Sentire surgical system in select markets outside the U.S. where the system is approved.

When it comes to making robotic surgeries more widely available in the U.S., Kamal said access comes down to three things: cost, training, and support.

“We are focused on all three. We are open to working with the hospitals on how we can create a financial value proposition for them to be able to adopt our system,” Kamal said. “Our goal is to bring the benefits of robotic surgery to many surgeons and patients around the world. Access is our number one priority.” 

Submit your innovation now!
