item.title: MassRobotics launching marine robotics facility on Boston Harbor
item.dc:creator: The Robot Report Staff
item.description:
MassRobotics plans to open the marine-focused facility in early 2028, with programming starting throughout 2027.

The post MassRobotics launching marine robotics facility on Boston Harbor appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
CRABI Robotics performs in-transit cleaning and inspection of marine vessels. | Source: MassRobotics

MassRobotics is developing a marine robotics facility at the historic Boston Fish Pier. The new facility will marine technology startups a space to build, launch and test robots on Boston Harbor. 

Construction is underway through a partnership with the Massachusetts Port Authority (Massport). MassRobotics plans to open the facility in early 2028, with programming starting throughout 2027.

“Boston has always been a harbor city, and some of today’s most exciting robotics work is happening in and under the water. Marine startups tell us that finding a place to test is one of their biggest hurdles,” said Tom Ryden, the executive director of MassRobotics. “With the Fish Pier steps from our headquarters, founders can build in our shop in the morning and test in the harbor by afternoon. We’re grateful to Massport for this partnership and excited to help make Boston a global center for marine robotics.”

The Fish Pier facility facility will be outfitted with testing equipment for marine robotics, including a water tank, a float alongside the pier for direct water testing, and lifting and launch equipment for getting vehicles in and out of the harbor. 

MassRobotics currently supports more than 100 resident startups from across the globe. The Fish Pier adds a new dimension to what it offers them and opens its doors wider to companies working in the blue economy. 

Submit your innovation now!

Access to water testing

Access to water for testing is often one of the biggest challenges for marine robotics startups. Testing an underwater vehicle or ocean sensor usually means renting boat time, borrowing a tank or traveling to a remote site. 

The Fish Pier facility removes that barrier. Companies can design and fabricate in the MassRobotics machine shop, then walk their prototype to the pier and put it in the harbor the same day. That tight loop between building and testing means faster iteration and lower costs for early-stage teams. 

CRABI Robotics, one of MassRobotics marine startups, develops an underwater hull-cleaning robot. It started as a three-person startup with an idea about how to make oceans cleaner. 

“For ocean startups, getting to the water is one of the hardest parts. A facility on the harbor, steps from where you build, will help the next marine company move a lot faster than we could,” said Levi Gershon, CEO of CRABI Robotics.

The post MassRobotics launching marine robotics facility on Boston Harbor appeared first on The Robot Report.

item.title: Robotics enters its post-Jensen Huang era
item.dc:creator: Steve Crowe
item.description:
One of robotics' most influential advocates is gone. Can the industry sustain its momentum without him?

The post Robotics enters its post-Jensen Huang era appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Jensen Huang keynote at CES 2025. | Credit: NVIDIA

Days before Christmas in 2023, Serve Robotics was on the verge of bankruptcy. A major investor pulled out of a committed funding round, leaving the developer of sidewalk delivery robots unable to make payroll and just days away from running out of cash.

With few options remaining, Serve Robotics co-founder and CEO Ali Kashani reached out to NVIDIA co-founder Jensen Huang. “We spoke at 6 a.m. the next day, and later that day I was having dinner with his executive team to find a way to bridge the company,” recalled Kashani. “Within days, they led a financing round that brought us back to life.”

Four months later, Serve Robotics was ringing the bell at Nasdaq to celebrate its public listing.

“I have heard similar stories from many other founders, as well as current and former NVIDIA employees, whose lives Jensen’s actions have changed,” Kashani said.

Over the past several years, few people outside the robotics industry have done more than Huang to elevate its profile.

Clad in his signature black leather jacket, Huang routinely dedicated portions of his marathon keynotes to robotics. He showcased humanoids on stage, introduced development tools, highlighted startups, championed open models and research, and made the case that robots would transform the world.

He also put NVIDIA’s money behind that vision.

Now, one of robotics’ most influential advocates is gone. NVIDIA’s board accepted Huang’s resignation on Nov. 12, and CFO Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO while the company searches for a permanent successor.

A large stage for robotics

For an industry that spent decades fighting for mainstream recognition, Huang provided something few robotics executives could: one of the biggest stages in technology.

“Jensen was fantastic in painting the vision,” said Yaro Tenzer, co-founder and CEO of RightHand Robotics.

Tenzer said Huang helped expand investors’ imaginations about what robotics could become.

NVIDIA said during its third-quarter earnings call that its physical AI revenue nearly tripled year over year and is on track to exceed $25 billion in fiscal 2027. While that represents a sizable and rapidly growing business, it still accounts for only about 6% of NVIDIA’s projected annual revenue of more than $400 billion. And physical AI encompasses more than robotics.

The attention Huang afforded robotics was disproportionate to its short-term commercial contribution.

“NVIDIA introduced its Isaac robotics platform back in 2017, and Jensen kept robotics in his keynotes and in the company’s long-term story year after year,” said Deepak Jayaraj, vice president of hardware engineering and manufacturing at agricultural robotics developer Four Growers. “I think that steady attention made it easier for founders to make the case to investors.”

Unlike Tesla CEO Elon Musk, whose robotics advocacy is largely centered on his own company’s products, Huang promoted an ecosystem of developers, many of whom compete directly with one another.

NVIDIA stood to benefit financially regardless of which robotics companies succeeded. But that business model also positioned Huang to become an advocate for the broader industry.

Providing infrastructure

Perhaps NVIDIA’s lasting contribution to robotics will be the development infrastructure it built under Huang. Its portfolio spans much of the robotics development stack, from GPUs and CUDA for AI training to Omniverse and Isaac Sim for simulation, Isaac Lab for robot learning, GR00T and Cosmos foundation models, Isaac ROS software, and Jetson embedded computing.

Jan Zizka, co-founder and CEO of warehouse robotics developer Brightpick and co-founder of machine vision specialist Photoneo, experienced NVIDIA’s impact firsthand. Zizka said Photoneo participated in an early-access program for NVIDIA’s Jetson TX1 computing platform.

“He was almost pushing the market to make it happen,” Zizka said, pointing to Huang’s willingness to invest in emerging markets before demand fully materialized.

NVIDIA’s investments in open research and software helped lower barriers to entry for developers. Zizka noted that its efforts in embedded computing also encouraged competitors, including AMD and Qualcomm, to pursue robotics opportunities.

Under Huang, NVIDIA became one of robotics’ most prominent strategic investors, backing companies including Figure AI, NEURA Robotics, Skild AI, Wayve, Waabi, and Serve Robotics. Beyond capital, an investment from NVIDIA provided an endorsement that could help startups attract additional investors, employees, and customers.

“Jensen’s style will be hard to copy,” said Jayaraj. “I’d judge whomever it is by which robotics programs they keep funding.”

“NVIDIA has a business reason to stay in, since many robot companies train and simulate on its compute long before they ship at scale,” he added. “The keynote time and the early bets on young teams are the parts that could fade.”

Losing an advocate inside NVIDIA

Huang’s enthusiasm for robotics was perhaps just as valuable inside NVIDIA as it was outside the company. Its robotics teams had an advocate at the highest level of the organization. Having earned considerable credibility with investors through previous long-term bets, Huang enjoyed a latitude his successor might not.

NVIDIA’s next CEO will also inherit growing competition in its core data center business and potentially greater political and regulatory scrutiny following the Democrats’ strong performance in the midterm elections.

Robert Little, co-founder and former CEO of ATI Industrial Automation, is particularly concerned about how opposition to data center construction could affect NVIDIA’s ability to fund its longer-term investments.

“Robotics is being propped up from the money that’s being created in the data centers for NVIDIA that affords NVIDIA to have a team of people developing product for robotics,” Little said.

If growth in that business slows, NVIDIA’s willingness to fund robotics research, product development, and strategic investments could be tested.

“What’s the first thing you do when you start to see a negative financial situation? You cut anything that’s not making money,” Little said.

Conversely, those pressures could make diversifying NVIDIA’s business even more important.

One early indicator of NVIDIA’s strategic priorities could be its pending $12.9 billion acquisition of Hugging Face, whose LeRobot initiative has become an important resource for robotics developers. Whether NVIDIA follows through on the deal will be worth watching, although regulatory hurdles could also influence its outcome.

NVIDIA has not responded to multiple requests for comment from The Robot Report about its robotics strategy following Huang’s departure. If we hear back, we will update this story. Huang’s son, Spencer, remains at NVIDIA, where he has worked for the past four and a half years. He has served as director of product management for robotics for the past 9 months.

The robotics flywheel is already spinning

Despite his concerns about NVIDIA’s data center business, Little believes the robotics industry has enough momentum to withstand the departure of any individual.

“The flywheel has been created and it is spinning now,” Little said. “We’re too far in. The momentum has been created, and now it’ll just carry itself through.”

Google DeepMind, Physical Intelligence, Generalist, Skild AI and many others are developing their own approaches to robot intelligence. Semiconductor companies are looking to challenge NVIDIA in embedded computing. Little argued that a less aggressive NVIDIA could benefit competing technology providers. And if robotics researchers and engineers were to leave NVIDIA, their expertise would likely find its way to other companies.

Tenzer similarly believes the physical AI movement has established considerable momentum.

“The foundations are there,” Tenzer said. “I think that things are really accelerating, and you can clearly see it.”

Zizka is more cautious, particularly about the potential ripple effects of disrupting the relationships and trust Huang helped build across the technology ecosystem.

“The best possible case is that it will continue,” Zizka said. “But I think this is a negative.”

Putting humanoids to the test

The bigger test, according to Tenzer, might come 12 months from now. Many humanoid developers have raised substantial funding based on expectations that advances in AI will unlock multi-purpose humanoids for industrial use.

“I think for the next year, maybe it will be fine,” Tenzer said. “But then I think a lot of these companies will struggle with showing actual use cases and real business.”

As companies return to investors seeking additional capital, Tenzer expects some of the enthusiasm surrounding humanoids to dissipate if commercial progress falls short of expectations.

“Somebody needs to get on that stage and show some of the cool things that are happening and have this charisma and have the ability to do it,” Tenzer said. “I think this is where Jensen will be missed.”

As with the autonomous vehicle investment boom, even failed humanoid startups could leave behind advances in manipulation, actuation, sensing, and robot learning that benefit the broader industry.

“Funding is where I’d watch first, especially for humanoid companies whose business case depends on breakthroughs that are still years out,” said Jayaraj. “Jensen’s advocacy gave those bets a lot of credibility.”

“Founders should ask how much of their plan rests on informal support or tools that haven’t shipped yet, because that kind of support can walk out the door with one person.”

Huang helped give companies such as Serve Robotics a chance to prove what was possible. With robotics enjoying unprecedented attention and investment, the industry’s next challenge is turning that attention into sustainable businesses.

The post Robotics enters its post-Jensen Huang era appeared first on The Robot Report.

item.title: What industrial drone deployments reveal about real-world autonomy challenges
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Metzelaar
item.description:
The engineering challenges of industrial drone autonomy include GNSS reliability, SLAM, sensor fusion, obstacle avoidance, and UAV validation.

The post What industrial drone deployments reveal about real-world autonomy challenges appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Supervised autonomous UAV inspection at an industrial facility. | Source: ZenaDrone

An autonomous drone can complete a carefully planned inspection route in a controlled environment and still struggle with the same route at an operating industrial facility. A steel structure may obstruct satellite signals, reflective equipment may distort depth measurements, and a wind gust may push the aircraft outside its planned trajectory. Each disturbance can be manageable in isolation. The difficulty emerges when several occur simultaneously. 

This exposes a fundamental challenge in industrial drone autonomy: performance depends on interactions between subsystems whose assumptions are rarely independent. 

A navigation algorithm may estimate position accurately under favorable sensing conditions. An obstacle detector may identify nearby structures during controlled testing. A flight controller may maintain stable tracking under a nominal payload. None of these results independently establishes that the integrated system can safely complete an inspection near energized infrastructure, confined structures, or operating machinery. 

Reliable deployment requires engineers to understand how uncertainty propagates through localization, perception, planning, control, and inspection-data acquisition. It also requires evidence that the system can recognize when its estimates are no longer trustworthy. 

Why industrial environments challenge autonomous navigation 

Industrial facilities introduce environmental conditions that are difficult to reproduce in laboratory demonstrations. 

Metallic surfaces, repetitive structural patterns, narrow access corridors, moving equipment, airborne particulates, and changing illumination can affect multiple sensors simultaneously. These conditions create both geometric constraints and uncertainty in the information available to the autonomy system. 

Consider a hypothetical UAV inspecting pipework beside a steel-framed processing facility. 

As the aircraft approaches the structure, GNSS measurements become less reliable. Repetitive pipes complicate visual feature matching, while reflective surfaces produce inconsistent depth observations. Meanwhile, the flight controller must reject aerodynamic disturbances caused by nearby structures. 

The resulting problem is not simply inaccurate positioning. The autonomy stack must decide whether its remaining localization confidence supports continued flight, whether detected free space is sufficiently reliable, and whether the planned maneuver remains dynamically feasible. 

These decisions are coupled. A localization error can corrupt obstacle coordinates, while a delayed perception update can cause the planner to act on geometry that no longer represents the aircraft’s surroundings. 

The practical engineering objective is therefore not uninterrupted autonomous operation under every condition. It is predictable behavior within a defined operational envelope, including when that envelope is exceeded. 

GNSS limitations and the localization problem 

Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) positioning provides an important absolute reference for outdoor autonomous UAV navigation. However, industrial structures introduce several failure mechanisms. 

Buildings, tanks, and overhead equipment can block direct satellite signals. Reflections from metallic surfaces create multipath interference, causing a receiver to process signals that have traveled indirect paths. 

Real-time kinematic (RTK) positioning can improve accuracy by using carrier-phase measurements and correction data. However, RTK does not eliminate obstruction, multipath, cycle slips, or poor satellite geometry. A fixed ambiguity solution should not be treated as an unconditional guarantee of accurate positioning. 

Combining absolute and relative localization

An inertial measurement unit (IMU) estimates angular velocity and specific force. Integrated inertial measurements support high-frequency motion propagation, but bias and noise cause errors to accumulate over time. 

Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) combines camera observations with inertial measurements to estimate relative motion. Published work such as VINS-Mono demonstrates nonlinear optimization approaches that integrate visual and inertial constraints for state estimation. 

Lidar-based odometry provides another approach, using geometric correspondence between successive scans. LIO-SAM, for example, combines lidar and inertial measurements in a factor-graph framework with mapping and loop-closure capabilities. 

These approaches have different weaknesses. Visual methods depend on illumination, image quality, and observable features. Lidar methods can struggle with insufficient geometric constraints, adverse returns, or sensor-specific limitations. 

Simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) additionally maintains a representation of the environment while estimating the robot’s pose. Loop closure can correct accumulated trajectory drift when a previously visited location is recognized, although incorrect associations can introduce significant map errors. 

For industrial UAVs, engineers must also distinguish local consistency from global accuracy. A drone may maintain a stable relative trajectory while its estimated position gradually diverges from the facility’s surveyed coordinate system. 

This distinction becomes critical when an inspection requires repeatable measurements at known asset locations. 

Obstacle avoidance is more than detecting objects 

Obstacle avoidance is often described as a perception problem. In operational UAV systems, it is an end-to-end timing and control problem. 

A typical pipeline must acquire sensor measurements, estimate obstacle geometry, update the local environment representation, generate a collision-free trajectory, and issue commands that the aircraft can physically execute. 

Each stage introduces latency and uncertainty. 

Sensor limitations affect the available flight envelope 

Lidar provides active range measurements and can support geometric mapping under varying visible-light conditions. However, transparent materials, highly reflective surfaces, thin wires, and unfavorable incidence angles can produce missing or misleading returns. 

Stereo vision estimates depth from image correspondence. Its performance depends on camera geometry, texture, illumination, and disparity estimation. Depth uncertainty generally increases with distance for a fixed stereo baseline and disparity uncertainty. 

Active depth cameras introduce their own range, illumination, interference, and surface-response constraints. 

No single sensing modality provides reliable coverage of every industrial obstacle. A practical design must account for sensor field of view, blind regions, minimum detection range, and the possibility that a hazard remains unobserved. 

Planning latency becomes physical distance 

For a simplified one-dimensional braking model, the distance required to respond to an obstacle can be approximated as: 

d_required ≈ vT + v²/(2a) 

Here, v is the aircraft’s speed toward the obstacle, T is the combined detection-to-control delay, and a is the achievable deceleration magnitude. 

This model assumes constant speed during the delay and constant deceleration afterward. It excludes additional clearance margins, uncertainty, wind, and complex multi-axis flight dynamics. 

Nevertheless, it illustrates why latency matters. Doubling flight speed doubles the distance traveled during processing delay and quadruples the idealized braking-distance term. 

A collision-avoidance system must therefore be evaluated against the aircraft’s actual maneuvering capability, not simply its obstacle detection range. 

Dynamic obstacles add another complication. A path considered clear at the beginning of a planning cycle may no longer be safe when the corresponding control command is executed. 

Sensor fusion and state estimation under real-world conditions 

Sensor fusion improves navigation by combining measurements with complementary characteristics. It also introduces dependencies that must be explicitly managed. 

An extended Kalman filter (EKF), commonly used for state estimation, propagates the system state through a motion model and corrects that prediction using sensor observations. 

The measurement update depends on the estimated uncertainty of both the prediction and the observations. If those uncertainty models are inaccurate, the filter may become overconfident. 

For example, GNSS measurements affected by multipath may exhibit correlated errors that are poorly represented by a simple independent-noise assumption. Accepting such measurements with excessive confidence can pull the state estimate away from the true trajectory. 

Innovation residuals and normalized innovation squared tests can help identify inconsistent measurements. However, statistical gating depends on appropriate noise models and does not guarantee detection of every failure. 

Calibration and synchronization are part of navigation 

A camera and IMU must have accurately characterized spatial transformations and timing relationships. 

Even a small temporal offset can create systematic visual-inertial estimation errors during rapid rotation. Incorrect extrinsic calibration can similarly produce inconsistent motion estimates. 

The Kalibr calibration framework provides established methods for estimating camera-IMU spatial and temporal relationships. 

Engineers should also monitor estimator consistency, covariance behavior, measurement rejection rates, and the duration for which the system can operate without reliable absolute position updates. 

A crucial distinction is that estimator covariance represents uncertainty under the assumed model. It is not necessarily a complete measure of actual error when the model itself is wrong. 

Environmental disturbances and flight control reliability 

Autonomous navigation cannot be separated from the aircraft’s flight dynamics. 

Wind gusts introduce external forces and moments that disturb trajectory tracking. Near buildings, airflow can become spatially variable, producing disturbances that differ from those encountered in unobstructed flight. For additional operational context, an overview of drone wind resistance levels provides a practical explanation of wind ratings and operating constraints; those ratings still require interpretation against aircraft configuration and site conditions. 

Payload changes affect mass, center of gravity, inertia, and power requirements. Vibration can degrade IMU measurements and camera image quality, particularly when mechanical isolation and filtering are insufficient. 

Actuator saturation creates another important limitation. A controller may calculate a corrective command that the motors cannot deliver because of thrust limits, battery voltage, or competing attitude-control demands. 

Control-loop stability must therefore be evaluated across expected payload configurations and operating conditions. 

Embedded computing introduces competing constraints 

Autonomous UAVs often execute localization, perception, mapping, planning, communications, and mission management on limited onboard computing resources. 

Higher-resolution sensing may improve geometric detail but increase processing load, memory use, power consumption, and latency. 

A computationally intensive SLAM update can also compete with perception or planning workloads. 

Engineers need to characterize worst-case execution times, deadline misses, scheduling behavior, and degraded-operation strategies rather than relying solely on average processor utilization. 

A navigation system that produces accurate estimates too late for the controller to use them is not operationally reliable. 

Why autonomous inspection data can still be unreliable 

Successfully navigating an inspection route does not guarantee that the resulting measurements are suitable for engineering decisions. 

Navigation accuracy and inspection-data accuracy are related but distinct. 

A UAV may maintain a stable position while capturing blurred imagery, poorly calibrated thermal measurements, or insufficiently overlapping photographs. 

For photogrammetric inspection, reconstruction quality depends on camera calibration, image geometry, surface texture, exposure, and the distribution of viewing angles. High image overlap alone cannot compensate for weak geometry or systematic calibration errors. 

Georeferencing adds further dependencies, including coordinate transformations, surveyed control, camera-to-body alignment, and synchronization between position estimates and image capture. 

Thermal imaging introduces different limitations. Apparent temperature depends on emissivity, reflected radiation, viewing geometry, atmospheric conditions, and instrument calibration. A thermal anomaly should not automatically be interpreted as a confirmed equipment defect. 

Lidar inspection similarly depends on scan geometry, range noise, incidence angle, point density, and motion compensation. 

For repeat inspections, engineers should evaluate whether the same physical feature can be measured consistently across missions. 

That requires separating repeatability from absolute accuracy and recording sufficient metadata to identify changes in sensing conditions. An inspection workflow should therefore validate both the flight trajectory and the quality of the collected engineering evidence. 

Human oversight, failure recovery, and operational safety 

Autonomous operation does not remove the need for supervisory control. 

A robust system should define the conditions under which it can continue, pause, return, land, or transfer authority to a human operator. 

These decisions require explicit fault-handling logic. 

Loss of GNSS alone may not justify terminating a mission if alternative localization remains sufficiently reliable. However, simultaneous localization degradation and restricted maneuvering space may make continued autonomous flight unacceptable. 

Return-to-home behavior also has limitations. It depends on available localization, a suitable return path, obstacle clearance, and sufficient energy. 

In a GNSS-denied or structurally confined environment, returning along a predefined route may be less appropriate than executing a separately validated contingency maneuver. 

Lost-link procedures should distinguish temporary communication interruption from broader navigation or control failures. 

Human intervention remains meaningful only when operators have adequate situational awareness, clear authority, and enough time to respond. 

For U.S. operations, engineering procedures must also align with applicable FAA requirements and authorizations. Autonomous mission execution does not independently remove regulatory responsibilities. 

The relevant safety question is not whether a UAV can fly without continuous manual input. It is whether the combined autonomous and supervisory system behaves acceptably when assumptions fail. 

How engineers should validate autonomous drone deployments 

Industrial deployment readiness cannot be established through a single successful demonstration. 

Testing should combine simulation, hardware-in-the-loop evaluation, controlled flight trials, and progressively representative operating environments. 

Simulation allows engineers to reproduce faults and explore scenarios that may be unsafe to introduce during early flight testing. However, simulated sensor models, aerodynamic disturbances, and environmental geometry cannot capture every physical effect. 

Field validation is needed to establish whether the assumptions used in simulation remain credible. 

Define measurable acceptance criteria 

A practical validation program should include metrics that connect algorithm behavior to operational outcomes. 

Engineering metric  What should be measured 
Localization error  Position and orientation error against an independent reference, including drift during degraded sensing 
Obstacle avoidance  Detection probability, missed hazards, clearance margins, and behavior across obstacle classes 
System latency  End-to-end sensing-to-action delay, including tail latency and deadline misses 
Mission completion  Successful completion under explicitly defined environmental and operational conditions 
Operator intervention  Frequency, cause, timing, and outcome of human intervention 
Failure recovery  Fault detection delay, transition behavior, and success of validated contingency procedures 
Inspection quality  Measurement accuracy, repeatability, image usability, and coverage of required assets 

These metrics require careful definitions. 

Localization error should be evaluated against an independent reference where feasible, rather than against the estimator’s own reported trajectory. Root-mean-square error alone may conceal short-duration excursions that are critical near obstacles. 

Obstacle detection performance should distinguish false positives from missed detections and account for obstacle size, material, distance, and approach geometry. 

Mission completion rates should report the tested scenario distribution and failure definitions. A high completion rate in benign conditions provides limited evidence about operation near industrial structures. 

Intervention frequency is useful only when the criteria for intervention and the level of autonomy are consistent. 

Test interactions between failures 

Individual fault tests are necessary but insufficient. 

A more revealing scenario might combine intermittent GNSS, reduced visual texture, increased processing latency, and moderate wind disturbances. 

The purpose is not to demonstrate that the UAV can tolerate every conceivable combination. It is to identify the boundaries within which the system remains controllable and capable of making trustworthy decisions. 

Engineers should document these boundaries as operational constraints, including conditions that trigger mission suspension or recovery. 

Reliable autonomy is a system-level property 

Industrial drone deployments expose the limitations of evaluating autonomy through isolated subsystem performance. 

Accurate localization does not guarantee safe obstacle avoidance. Successful obstacle avoidance does not guarantee stable flight control. Stable flight does not guarantee useful inspection measurements. And successful mission execution does not demonstrate that the system will respond appropriately to degraded sensing or unexpected faults. 

Reliable autonomy emerges when sensing, estimation, planning, control, data acquisition, and human supervision are designed and validated together. 

For robotics engineers, the central challenge is not merely improving individual algorithms. It is establishing measurable operating boundaries, understanding how errors propagate between subsystems, and ensuring that the aircraft can recognize and respond when its assumptions no longer hold. 

That is the difference between demonstrating autonomous flight and engineering an autonomous system suitable for industrial operations. 

Submit your innovation now!

About the Author

Jonathan Metzelaar is a contributor associated with ZenaDrone Inc., a company working in unmanned aerial systems. His contribution examines technical considerations in autonomous UAV navigation, sensing, and industrial deployment.

The post What industrial drone deployments reveal about real-world autonomy challenges appeared first on The Robot Report.

item.title: Humyn Labs raises $47M to collect real-world data for robotics
item.dc:creator: Brianna Wessling
item.description:
Humyn Labs provides data collected from real-world operations for frontier AI labs, robotics companies, and world-model developers.

The post Humyn Labs raises $47M to collect real-world data for robotics appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Humyn Labs’ co-founders, from left to right, Ishank Gupta and Manish Agarwal. | Source: Humyn Labs

Humyn Labs, a physical AI research and deployment company, today announced it raised $47 million in Series A funding. The company said it has also surpassed $50 million in annualized revenue within six months of operations. 

Humyn Labs works with frontier AI labs, robotics companies and world-model developers. It uses its own data capture and enrichment operations across over 20 countries to help robots better prepare for deployments in the real world. 

“A lot of robotics development is bottlenecked in terms of what’s happening in the real world. A bunch of the robotics development that we were seeing and a bunch of the partners that we were talking to were working on essentially simulated environments,” Ishank Gupta, the co-founder of Humyn Labs, told The Robot Report. “The biggest gap was how do you take what’s happening in the lab into the real world?”

The funding round includes $26 million in equity led by Accel. It included participation from Prosus Ventures, BeeGlobal, Finserv Intelligence through Bajaj Finance, Bajaj Alts AI Opportunities Fund, Dallas Venture Capital, Lighthouse Canton, Jump Trading LLC and marquee angel investor Anita Pramoda, former CFO of Epic. The $21 million venture debt round was led by Lighthouse Canton with participation from Trifecta Capital. 

Humyn Labs gathers data across four modalities

Right now, Humyn Labs gathers data across vision, sound, touch, and motion. “The idea is to not just be a data partner, but also a deployment partner to our customers,” Gupta said. The company gathers data using its proprietary capture devices.

These devices record how people perform specific jobs to a specific labs’ requirements. Meanwhile, Humyn Labs’ end-to-end data engine converts these into labelled, training-ready datasets with verified provenance across these four modalities. 

“We want to be an extension of the lab’s research team. We work backwards from what the researchers need, and then build out bespoke large-scale collection programs and enrichment programs,” Gupta said. “We currently operate and partner with on-ground collection partners across 20 countries. Our biggest area of operations are LATAM, southeast Asia, south Asia, and east Asia.” 

For audio data, Gupta said the company focuses on gathering data across different languages rather than across different industries. Vision, touch, and motion data, however, typically go hand in hand and are more industry specific.

Humyn Labs’ data can be applied to a range of industries. The company divides the industries it works in into three overarching categories: residential, commercial, and industrial. 

“The distinction between commercial and industrial is anything manufacturing or anything factory sits in industrial. Anything outside that sits in commercial. Warehousing, retail, hospitality, all of that will sit in commercial,” Gupta said.

A chart showing how Humyn Labs’ data engine works. | Source: Humyn Labs

Working across different robot embodiments

Humyn Labs’ isn’t interested in deciding how end-users should automate tasks, so its data can be useful across a range of robot embodiments. 

“We work across embodiments, because the focus is on understanding how certain tasks can be done. Robot arms are amazing for any task that requires manipulation but doesn’t require navigation. Those are amazing in industrial environments or in an assembly line setup or any other setup where a person has a stationary task where they don’t need to move,” Gupta said. 

This is especially important in industrial environments. Meanwhile, in commercial environments, you see more tasks that require manipulation and navigation.

“If you are working in a hotel, for example, or in a warehouse, you have to do manipulation but also move around,” Gupta said. Home environments, he continued, include a mix of these kinds of tasks. 

“Different labs have different thought processes on embodiments. There are some labs that are working on building a brain, which could be embodiment agnostic. Most of your frontier labs sit in that bucket, and then there are embodiment-specific robotics companies. So, we work across a spectrum,” Gupta said.

Submit your innovation now!

What are Humyn Labs’ plans for the funding?

The funding will support three areas: deployment readiness infrastructure in Brazil, Korea and India; the company’s capture hardware and enrichment engine; and on-the-ground presence in San Francisco, London and Seoul. The team hopes to make it so robotics labs can spend more time focusing on important work. 

“When the stakes are so high, and the models are evolving so fast, why would a lab waste time ensuring that certain hardware reaches a site in Venezuela, and then that operators are collecting that data,” Manish Agarwal, the co-founder of Humyn Labs, said. “I would rather have high impact work happening with the best of the research scientists so that I can compete.”

Additionally, the company hopes to accelerate deployment readiness. Agarwal said right now, the robotics industry is in a place where its still figuring out how long the average deployment cycle might be. 

“We see that as an opportunity rather than a challenge. For deployment readiness, the biggest gap is this whole real-sim-real flywheel, and with every percentage improvement, we will really need that flywheel to work faster and deeper,” Agarwal said. To make this happen, the industry needs the right data, and the right data partner, he said. 

The post Humyn Labs raises $47M to collect real-world data for robotics appeared first on The Robot Report.

item.title: From Commercial Scale to Embodied Intelligence: The Next Challenge for Robotics
item.dc:creator: Sponsored Content
item.description:
Robotics is advancing rapidly. New AI models and increasingly capable hardware are expanding what machines can perceive, understand and do.

The post From Commercial Scale to Embodied Intelligence: The Next Challenge for Robotics appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Robotics is advancing rapidly. New AI models and increasingly capable hardware are expanding what machines can perceive, understand and do, bringing more adaptable and general-purpose robots closer to practical use.

But greater capability does not automatically translate into commercial readiness. In supermarkets, hotels, airports and other working environments, robots must navigate changing conditions, operate alongside people, integrate with existing workflows and perform reliably over time. The challenge is not simply what a robot can do, but whether it can do it consistently and at scale.

Pudu Robotics Product Portfolio

That challenge was a central theme at Pudu Robotics‘ European Partner Summit in Amsterdam on November 4. Under the theme “AI in Action: Scaling Impact Across Europe — Together,” the company brought together its six product lines, spanning commercial delivery, commercial cleaning, industrial delivery, general embodied AI, commercial lawn care and home lawn care. The portfolio reflected a broader strategic direction: connecting the company’s experience in commercial robotics with its expanding work in embodied intelligence through One Brain, Multiple Embodiments.

Pudu Robotics European Partner Summit

For the robotics industry, this highlights an important relationship between two developments often considered separately: the experience of deploying specialized robots at scale, and the pursuit of more adaptable intelligence across different machines.

Commercial Scale as a Foundation for Robotics

Real-world deployment exposes robots to challenges that controlled testing cannot fully capture. A supermarket cleaning robot must operate around shoppers and changing floor conditions. A hotel delivery robot needs to navigate shared spaces and interact with elevators. In manufacturing environments, autonomous mobile robots must move materials reliably within established workflows.

Addressing these challenges requires more than navigation algorithms. It involves hardware engineering, perception, fleet management, system integration and the service infrastructure needed to support long-term operation.

Pudu Robotics, a global leader in commercial robotics, has shipped more than 130,000 robots across over 85 countries and regions, serving more than 50,000 customers in over 1,000 cities. Its deployment footprint spans a range of industries, with customers including Denner, EDEKA, Albert Heijn, Carrefour, Marriott, Van der Valk and Paris Charles de Gaulle Airport.

PUDU CC1 at Denner

The scale of these operations is reflected in the breadth of environments served. Denner, the Swiss supermarket chain within Migros Group, expanded its deployment of PUDU CC1 commercial cleaning robots from an initial four-store pilot to approximately 200 units. In hospitality, Pudu robots support service workflows at hotels such as Van der Valk. Across these settings, successful deployment depends not only on task performance, but also on how well robots fit into existing operations and maintain consistent performance in daily use.

Such deployments provide more than commercial validation. They build practical engineering experience in handling environmental variability, human interaction, workflow integration and operational reliability. Field experience and customer feedback also inform product refinement over time. These capabilities are difficult to develop in isolation: they emerge through the repeated process of deploying, supporting and improving robots in real working environments.

As robotics moves toward more general-purpose applications, this accumulated experience becomes an important foundation for tackling a broader range of tasks and environments.

One Brain, Multiple Embodiments: A Shared Foundation for Embodied AI

A central challenge in embodied AI is how to extend capabilities beyond individual machines. Different robot forms have traditionally required substantial hardware and software adaptation, making it difficult to reuse capabilities and scale development across platforms.

Pudu’s One Brain, Multiple Embodiments strategy is designed to address this challenge through a shared technological architecture built around two core technologies: PuduFM and PuduAgent.

One Brain, Multiple Embodiments Architecture

PuduFM is Pudu’s embodied intelligence foundation model, developed around the concept of physical intuition. Beyond recognizing objects or following predefined instructions, it is designed to help robots understand spatial structures, reason about physical relationships and anticipate changes in the physical world. These capabilities are important to moving beyond predefined task execution toward more context-aware interaction with physical environments.

PuduAgent complements this foundation as a universal embodied AI agent platform for the physical world. It provides a framework for organizing and deploying embodied intelligence capabilities, with reusable skills and safety mechanisms that support application development across robotic platforms.

Together, PuduFM and PuduAgent underpin an architecture built around three core technology areas: Embodied Navigation, Embodied Manipulation and Embodied Interaction. The aim is to make selected AI capabilities, software modules and skills reusable across different robot forms, while allowing hardware and motion-control systems to remain optimized for specific tasks.

As Felix Zhang, founder and CEO of Pudu Robotics, put it at the Amsterdam summit, “The next stage of growth will depend not only on advancing robot capabilities, but also on making robots easier to deploy, more adaptable and commercially viable at scale.”

That perspective reflects the practical rationale behind the strategy. A cleaning robot, an industrial mobile robot and a humanoid do not need identical bodies or motion systems. What can be shared is the underlying intelligence and selected capabilities, adapted to different hardware and operating requirements. The objective is not to make every robot interchangeable, but to reduce the need to develop every capability from scratch for each new platform.

Pudu’s embodied AI portfolio includes the PUDU D5 quadruped, PUDU D7 semi-humanoid and PUDU D9 humanoid, alongside its established specialized robots. These platforms represent different approaches to mobility, physical interaction and task execution. The shared architecture provides a framework for extending capabilities across them as technology matures.

Expanding Robotics Across Applications and Markets

The same combination of specialized engineering and shared technological foundations also creates room to expand into new applications. Building on its experience in commercial delivery and cleaning, Pudu is moving beyond indoor commercial environments into outdoor and residential settings.

The recent launches of the PUDU GT series of commercial lawn care robots and the PUDU TOMO S series for home lawn care mark this expansion — extending autonomous robotics from indoor to outdoor environments, and from commercial use into the home. These are not simply new product categories. They reflect how capabilities developed through specialized robotics can be applied to an increasingly diverse range of real-world tasks.

Years of developing and deploying robots in diverse real-world environments have given Pudu experience in task-specific engineering, system integration and large-scale operations. Combined with the One Brain, Multiple Embodiments architecture, this experience provides a basis for extending its portfolio into new applications while reusing relevant technologies and development capabilities. The approach connects the company’s established commercial robotics business with its longer-term ambition to build more adaptable embodied intelligence.

Turning this broader portfolio into sustained adoption also requires a strong regional presence. Pudu operates in more than 20 European countries and has reported average annual revenue growth of over 60% across the region over the past two years. In October 2026, the company announced the establishment of its European headquarters in Neuss, Germany, bringing together sales, showroom, warehousing, training and after-sales support capabilities.

For customers considering larger deployments, local technical support, partner networks and service capabilities are essential to operational continuity. Regional infrastructure is therefore not separate from product innovation; it is part of what makes robotics deployable and commercially viable across markets.

The Next Challenge: Making Intelligence Work in the Physical World

The next phase of robotics will not be defined by AI capabilities alone, but by the ability to translate intelligence into reliable, scalable systems that work in the physical world.

For Pudu, the journey toward more general-purpose robotics builds on a foundation established through years of commercial deployment. By combining proven engineering and commercialization capabilities with advances in embodied intelligence, Pudu is working to extend robotics across more forms, tasks and environments.

The future of robotics is not simply about building machines that can do more. It is about making intelligent robots work reliably, create tangible value and become an increasingly natural part of how people work and live.

item.title: Rockwell Automation acquiring mobile robot maker AGILOX
item.dc:creator: Steve Crowe
item.description:
Rockwell Automation has agreed to acquire autonomous mobile robot developer AGILOX, expanding its mobile robotics portfolio following its 2023 acquisition of OTTO Motors.

The post Rockwell Automation acquiring mobile robot maker AGILOX appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
An AGILOX mobile robot operating inside a container. | Credit: AGILOX

Rockwell Automation has signed a definitive agreement to acquire AGILOX, an Austria-based developer of autonomous mobile robots (AMRs). Rockwell said the acquisition will more than double the size of its AMR business and complement its existing OTTO Motors portfolio.

Financial terms of the acquisition were not disclosed. The deal is expected to close in the second quarter of Rockwell’s fiscal 2027, subject to regulatory approval. AGILOX will become part of Rockwell’s Intelligent Devices operating segment.

AGILOX said it has deployed more than 2,500 AMRs worldwide since its founding in 2017. The company has more than 250 employees and operations in Europe, North America, and China. Its robots are used in automotive, third-party logistics, food and beverage, and pharmaceutical applications.

The acquisition will combine OTTO’s strong presence in North America with AGILOX’s established customer base in Europe, Rockwell said.

The acquisition also marks an exit for global investment firm Carlyle, which made a majority growth investment in AGILOX in 2021. According to Carlyle, AGILOX has quadrupled its revenue since then and launched a robots-as-a-service (RaaS) offering.

How AGILOX and OTTO Motors compare

Both AGILOX and OTTO Motors develop AMRs that automate material transport. However, there are several differences between their technologies.

OTTO specializes in flatbed AMRs that can be equipped with attachments such as conveyors and lift tables to transport different materials. Its largest AMR, the OTTO 1500, can carry payloads of up to 1,900 kg (4,189 lb.). The company also offers an autonomous forklift called OTTO Lifter.

AGILOX specializes in AMRs with integrated lifting mechanisms for transporting pallets and other loads. Its robots feature omnidirectional drives, enabling them to move sideways and diagonally without turning. This allows the robots to maneuver in tight spaces. AGILOX also has an autonomous forklift.

Submit your innovation now!

Rockwell said the technologies are complementary, but it did not disclose how it plans to integrate the two platforms or whether customers will eventually be able to operate AGILOX and OTTO robots as part of the same fleet.

Rockwell continues to expand its robotics business

The AGILOX deal comes three years after Rockwell acquired Clearpath Robotics, including its industrial division, OTTO Motors. Rockwell valued that acquisition at $609 million at the time of purchase.

Founded in 2009 in Ontario, Canada, Clearpath initially developed mobile robots for research applications. It launched OTTO Motors in 2015 to automate material handling in industrial environments.

Rockwell has also invested in robotics beyond AMRs. In March 2025, it made a strategic investment in RightHand Robotics, a Massachusetts-based developer of robotic piece-picking systems for warehouses. Financial terms of that investment were not disclosed. RightHand Robotics combines AI, machine vision, and robotic gripping to pick individual items in fulfillment operations.

item.title: California DMV bars Waymo AVs from operating on the state’s freeways
item.dc:creator: Brianna Wessling
item.description:
The DMV determined that Waymo's freeway operations "pose an imminent hazard to public safety due to recurring incursions by its vehicles."

The post California DMV bars Waymo AVs from operating on the state’s freeways appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Waymo said the DMV order only applies to freeways and will not affect its operations on city streets. | Source: Waymo

The California Department of Motor Vehicles has barred Waymo autonomous vehicles (AVs) from operating on the state’s freeways. The DMV issued the order on Nov. 11, following a number of incidents in the state, it confirmed to The Robot Report.

Waymo said it will restrict freeway operations across all of its operating areas, as part of its safety-first approach.

The ban comes “following an incident in which three Waymo autonomous vehicles entered an active construction closure on U.S. Route 101 near Burlingame and another incident involving CHP vehicles on Highway 280 in San Francisco,” the DMV said. In the second incident, a Waymo vehicle can be seen attempting to drive past California Highway Patrol officers while they’re conducting a traffic stop. You can watch the incidents below.

The DMV determined that Waymo’s freeway operations “pose an imminent hazard to public safety due to recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones where construction workers, vehicles and equipment are present.” The action prevents Waymo from operating or testing its driverless vehicles on all California freeways.

The restrictions will remain in place until Waymo demonstrates to the DMV that it has “taken effective corrective actions to address the deficiencies that precipitated the restrictions.” This includes providing evidence that its AVs can safely detect and respond to construction zones, emergency vehicles, and other roadway situations within the vehicles’ operational design domain.

“Safety is at the foundation of everything we do. Following recent freeway construction zone encounters on U.S. 101 in California that did not involve any injuries or collisions, the California DMV has implemented an operating restriction on freeway operations in the state. In alignment with our safety-first principles, we have also temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets to evaluate our performance. Our ride-hailing service continues to operate safely on surface streets, serving over half a million trips each week. We are working with the California DMV and other state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations,” a Waymo spokesperson told The Robot Report.

Waymo AVs struggle with construction zones

This isn’t Waymo’s first time running into issues with the California DMV this year. The DMV noted that Waymo AVs still posed a safety threat “despite a prior restriction and corrective actions implemented following similar incidents that occurred on May 18, 2026.”

The incidents the DMV is referring to occurred when seven Waymo vehicles drove between construction cones and into closed lanes in San Francisco. This incident resulted in Waymo issuing a safety recall with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) in June.

In the recall report, Waymo said that “under certain circumstances, the AV may enter and drive at speed in freeway construction zones due to inappropriately prioritizing the avoidance of other freeway hazards and/or failing to recognize the construction zone.” The recall was supposed to enhance Waymo AVs’ performance in and around freeway construction zones.

Waymo said it plans to continue freeway testing with trained autonomous specialists in the vehicles. It noted that its vehicles had been driving fully autonomously on California freeways for several years and began offering public riders trips using freeways last November.

Emergency vehicles, stopped school buses, and now construction zones have been some of the biggest challenges for Waymo since it began rolling out its robotaxis in 2018. Waymo now operates commercial services in over 15 cities in the U.S., including Austin, Las Vegas, and Atlanta. It has plans to expand to 17 more cities, including in London and Tokyo, in the coming years.

Waymo vehicles and hit-and-runs in Arizona

The robotaxis have also been involved in a growing number of hit-and-run incidents in Arizona, according to a local CBS channel.

Almost half of all police-reported crashes involving Waymo robotaxis in the Phoenix metro area end with the human driver fleeing the scene—a hit-and-run rate per mile more than double that of the general public, according to a 10-month review of crash reports and body-camera footage.

item.title: Learn how AI is changing supply chain robotics
item.dc:creator: The Robot Report Staff
item.description:
The live webinar, "Robots in the Supply Chain," will take place Wednesday, November 18, 2026, at 12 P.M. ET.

The post Learn how AI is changing supply chain robotics appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
From left to right: Lior Elazary, the co-founder and CEO of inVia Robotics, Josip Cesic, the co-founder and CEO of Gideon, and Jeff Mahler, the co-founder and CTO of Ambi Robotics.

Supply chain robotics is undergoing rapid transformation. Companies hope to address labor shortages, improve efficiency, and build resilience against disruptions. Increasingly, they’re turning to robotics to solve these challenges.

Currently, available technologies include warehouse automation, picking and packing systems, autonomous mobile robots for material handling, and AI-powered inventory management. These systems can work together and help organizations adapt to changing demand patterns and product variations.

Now, the integration of artificial intelligence is enabling predictive analytics, demand forecasting, and dynamic routing optimization. With AI, robots can learn from operational data to improve performance, reduce errors, and optimize energy consumption.

Even manufacturers already using robots stand to gain from these advancements, achieving higher quality, reduced downtime, better predictability, and cost optimization. This transition is a strategic necessity, supporting the shift towards high-volume, high-mix production and resilient supply chains.

Learn about all of the latest advancements in the webinar, “Robots in the Supply Chain.” The live webinar will take place Wednesday, November 18, 2026, at 12 P.M. ET. If you can’t attend live, registered attendees will be able to watch a recording of the webinar at their convenience.

The webinar will feature insights from three robotics experts: Lior Elazary, co-founder and CEO of InVia Robotics; Josip Cesic, co-founder and CEO of Gideon; and Jeff Mahler, co-founder and CTO of Ambi Robotics.

In this webinar, attendees will learn how:

  • Integrated automation solutions combine warehouse robotics, AI, and predictive analytics for end-to-end supply chain optimization.
  • AI-powered systems enable adaptive operations that respond to changing demand patterns and disruptions.
  • High-volume, high-mix production requirements drive adoption of flexible robotic solutions.
  • Real-time visibility and predictive capabilities improve decision-making and operational resilience.

Meet the speakers

Lior Elazary is the co-founder and CEO of inVia Robotics. At inVia, he leads the company’s vision for applying AI, software, and robotics to improve warehouse operations. With more than 20 years of experience in technology and entrepreneurship, he has built and scaled companies across robotics, software, networking, and enterprise technology.

Josip Cesic is the co-founder and CEO of Gideon, a pioneering robotics and AI company. Gideon revolutionizes supply chains with their Physical-AI platform, automating some of the hardest automation problems such as loading and unloading truck trailers with autonomous forklifts.

Cesic holds a PhD in autonomy technologies from the University of Zagreb (FER), Croatia, and completed with the University of Waterloo, Canada. His accolades include the Dean’s Award, Special Dean’s Award, Rector’s Award, Special Rector’s Award, and the Silver Plaque for his outstanding doctoral dissertation. He holds several patents and has published over 20 research papers on robotics and AI. Josip also serves on the Board of Alumni at FER.

Jeff Mahler is a co-founder and the CTO for Ambi Robotics, previously serving as CEO of the company. Mahler is responsible for guiding the vision and execution of the company’s advanced operating system, AmbiOS, to power highly dexterous robotic systems in commercial production.

Mahler obtained his Ph.D. from UC Berkeley as a member of the AUTOLAB and Berkeley Artificial Intelligence Research Lab. His dissertation research is on the Dexterity-Network (Dex-Net), and he has also published on deep learning from demonstration and control for surgical robots. His research papers have been nominated for numerous awards, including Best Manipulation Paper (ICRA 2016) and Best Human-Robot Interaction Paper (ICRA 2016).

Mahler’s open-source code, training datasets, and neural network weights receive hundreds of downloads per month. Along with Prof. Ruzena Bajcsy, he helped start EE 106B, the UC Berkeley course on mathematical models for robot manipulation. Previously, he co-founded the 3D scanning startup Lynx Laboratories in 2012, which was acquired by Occipital, Inc., and he received the National Defense Science and Engineering Fellowship in 2015.
